title: Practice Set PRS2 — Custom Catalyst Rules
description: Senior applied-architecture track: diagnose a custom Catalyst rule that misfires, and tell when to use a hint rather than a rule. Companion to PSS1.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Senior plan-reading scenarios describe GridUnion Continental at platform scale (850M meters across 4 countries, 30 regions, 6 teams, 8TB+ archive); the CSV itself is a small sample for schema reference.
Substations reference. Anchors cross-team architectural scenarios.

tasks.title: The Custom Rule That Misfires

description.context: GridUnion's Risk team registered a custom Catalyst rule six months ago. The rule's intent was to push regulatory country-filter predicates into nested subqueries for jurisdictional isolation — country='DE' should isolate German positions early in the plan to prevent accidental data exposure. Reporting team's daily aggregation pipeline started producing wrong results last week. Their plan shows the Risk team's rule firing on Reporting's join query — a query that has nothing to do with regulatory isolation. The architect reads the rule's predicate match.
description.task: What is the architectural problem with how this rule is registered, and what is the fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Rule Name: RegulatoryCountryFilterPushdown

Rule Intent: Risk team's regulatory isolation

Rule Match Predicate: any plan containing a Filter operator referencing a 'country' column

Incident: Reporting team's join query produced wrong results last week

Reporting Query: joins customer_dim (which has a 'country' column) with positions; rule injected a filter that the query never asked for

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: A custom Catalyst rule registered cluster-wide whose match predicate is too broad and fires on unrelated team's queries

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Risk team's rule (registered cluster-wide as a Catalyst extension)
class RegulatoryCountryFilterPushdown extends Rule[LogicalPlan] {
  override def apply(plan: LogicalPlan): LogicalPlan = plan transform {
    case f @ Filter(_, _) if planContainsColumn(f, "country") =>
      injectCountryIsolation(f)  // wraps with regulatory partitioning logic
  }
}

# Reporting's plan with rule fired (unintended)
+- HashAggregate(keys=[region], functions=[sum(daily_kw)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, 800)
      +- Project [region, daily_kw]
         +- Filter ((country = 'DE') AND (some other condition))   ← injected by rule
            +- SortMergeJoin [customer_id], [customer_id], Inner
               :- FileScan parquet positions
               +- FileScan parquet customer_dim    ← contains 'country' column

# Reporting's actual code (no country filter requested)
result = positions.join(customer_dim, on='customer_id').groupBy('region').sum('daily_kw')

fields.label: What is the architectural problem with how this rule is registered, and what is the fix?
options: Custom rules cannot be registered cluster-wide in Spark 3.5; this is a misconfiguration. Fix: move the rule into Risk's session-only extensions config so it does not affect other teams' SparkSessions.

The injected filter is correct — Reporting's customer_dim includes German customers and the regulatory rule MUST fire. Fix: Reporting team adjusts their query to filter country before joining customer_dim.

Rules registered as Catalyst extensions cannot be cross-team safe; the rule registration itself is the problem. Fix: revoke Risk's permission to register Catalyst rules. Custom rules should be Platform-team-only.
The rule's match predicate is too broad — ANY query touching ANY table with a country column triggers it. Fix: scope the match to specific table identities OR convert to opt-in query hint.
fields.correctAnswer: The rule's match predicate is too broad — ANY query touching ANY table with a country column triggers it. Fix: scope the match to specific table identities OR convert to opt-in query hint.
fields.rationale: Predicate scope governs which queries a registered rule will affect. Risk's intent was regulatory isolation for THEIR queries against THEIR regulatory tables. The fix has two paths. Tighten the match: scope to specific table identities (e.g., only fire when the source table is risk.regulatory_positions). Convert to opt-in: rewrite as a query hint /*+ REGULATORY_ISOLATION */ that teams apply when needed. The opt-in version (PRS2.2) is generally the safer choice for cross-team-shared infrastructure.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats registration scope as the issue; the issue is match-predicate scope.

Option B: Treats the wrong-fire as correct. Reporting's query never asked for regulatory filtering.

Option C: Generalizes to 'no custom rules'; some teams need them. Tighter match works.

tasks.pssReference: PSS2 lesson 7 (Catalyst Extension Architecture), PSS9 lesson 6 (Cross-Team Risk in Custom Rules).

tasks.title: Hint, Not Rule

description.context: After PRS2.1 surfaced the misfire problem, GridUnion's architecture council debates how to encode the regulatory isolation rule. The Risk team's senior engineer proposes two implementations side by side: as a custom Catalyst Rule (always fires when match conditions hold) or as a Query Hint /*+ REGULATORY_ISOLATION */ (opt-in, applies only when callers add the hint). The architect must compare them and identify which is the safer architectural pattern for cross-team-shared infrastructure.
description.task: Which is the safer architectural choice on a shared cluster, and what is the structural reason?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Implementation A: Custom Rule registered cluster-wide; fires automatically when plan-shape matches

Implementation B: Custom Hint registered cluster-wide; fires only when /*+ REGULATORY_ISOLATION */ appears in caller's query

Shared Cluster: true (6 teams)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two implementations of the same optimization — as Rule vs as Hint — compared for cross-team safety properties

evidence.label: Implementation A — as Rule (Risk team's original proposal)
Implementation B — as Hint (the architect's counter-proposal)
evidence.content:
class RegulatoryHint extends QueryHintProvider {
  override def hintName: String = "REGULATORY_ISOLATION"
  override def apply(hinted: LogicalPlan): LogicalPlan =
    injectCountryIsolation(hinted)
}

# Cluster registration:
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.queryHintProviders', 'com.gridunion.RegulatoryHint')

# Behavior: fires ONLY when caller writes /*+ REGULATORY_ISOLATION */.
# Risk team's own queries always include the hint; other teams never do.
# Risk team usage:
#   spark.sql("SELECT /*+ REGULATORY_ISOLATION */ * FROM risk.positions ...")

fields.label: Which is the safer architectural choice on a shared cluster, and what is the structural reason?
options: Implementation A — Rules are more reliable than Hints because they cannot be forgotten by callers. The PRS2.1 misfire would not have happened if the rule's match predicate had been narrower; the Rule pattern itself is fine.

Implementation B — Hints are opt-in by construction. Teams not regulated by the rule will not include the hint and the optimization will not fire. Cross-team risk is structurally eliminated; Risk team explicitly opts in for their own queries.

Both implementations have equivalent risk profiles; the difference is naming. Convert either back to the simplest form (an SQL CASE WHEN inside the query body) to avoid Catalyst-extension complexity entirely.

Neither — both create cross-team coupling because they share the cluster Catalyst registry. The architect should require Risk to run a separate SparkSession with its own optimizer extensions, isolated from other teams entirely.
fields.correctAnswer: Implementation B — Hints are opt-in by construction. Teams not regulated by the rule will not include the hint and the optimization will not fire. Cross-team risk is structurally eliminated; Risk team explicitly opts in for their own queries.
fields.rationale: Opt-in semantics is the structural property distinguishing the two patterns. Rules fire on plan-shape match, which means a too-broad match predicate produces silent cross-team impact (PRS2.1). Even with a tightened match, future code changes to ANY team's tables can re-trigger the issue. The hint pattern shifts the responsibility to the caller, which is correct architecture: the team that wants the optimization opts into it. Risk team always adds /*+ REGULATORY_ISOLATION */ to THEIR queries; other teams never write the hint and are unaffected.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Conflates 'rules can be made safe' with 'rules are safer'. Hints are structurally safer.

Option C: Treats Catalyst extensions as avoidable; they exist for legitimate reasons.

Option D: Suggests separate SparkSessions; on shared infrastructure that's neither feasible nor scalable.

tasks.pssReference: PSS2 lesson 7-8 (Catalyst Extensions vs Query Hints).
